chapter_name: Terms, Concepts and their Use in Sociology
learning_objective: 🎯 Learn the special 'language' of sociology—the terms and concepts we use to decode human behavior, social ranking, and group dynamics!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: A social group consists of two or more people who interact regularly and share a sense of identity. Primary groups (family, close friends) are small and emotional. Secondary groups (school, office) are large and task-oriented.

Status is the position you hold in society (e.g., student, doctor). Role is the behavior expected from that status (e.g., a student studies). 'Ascribed' status is by birth (caste, gender), while 'Achieved' status is earned (degree, job).

The system by which society ranks categories of people in a hierarchy. It creates structural inequalities. The main forms are Caste (closed system based on birth), Class (open system based on wealth), Estate, and Slavery.
The methods society uses to regulate human behavior and maintain order. Formal control includes laws, police, and courts. Informal control includes gossip, smiles, frowns, and family scoldings.
An 'In-group' is a group you belong to and feel loyalty toward ('Us'). An 'Out-group' is a group you don't belong to and might feel rivalry toward ('Them').

fun_activity.title: 🎭 The Status Matrix
fun_activity.instructions: Make a list of 5 'Statuses' you hold right now (e.g., Daughter, Student, Football Captain, Teenager, Indian). Next to each, write if it is 'Ascribed' (given by birth) or 'Achieved' (earned by you)!

exam_tips: 📌 Distinguish clearly between Primary Group (face-to-face, permanent) and Secondary Group (impersonal, temporary).
📌 Remember: 'You OCCUPY a status, but you PLAY a role.'
📌 Caste is an 'ascribed' status (cannot be changed), whereas Class is an 'achieved' status (can be changed through effort).
quick_recap: ⭐ A crowd is a mere collection of people (aggregate), while a group has interaction and a sense of belonging.
⭐ Role conflict happens when the demands of two different roles clash (e.g., working mother).
⭐ Social control uses both rewards (positive sanctions) and punishments (negative sanctions).
